newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil complex ends weaker in sideways market.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil complex ends weaker in sideways market.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil futures prices ended mostly lower Friday after a quiet day of sideways trading, digesting the week's price swings with mild profit taking while awaiting some clear motivation, traders said.
Refined products closed lower also, weakening alongside crude as well through spread trades tied to Friday's expiration of the spot June contracts in unleaded gas and heating oil.
Crude oil for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange closed 9 cents lower at $20.88 a barrel after rising 18 cents on Thursday.
July unleaded gasoline lost 0.44 cent to settle at 62.81 cents a gallon. July heating oil closed at 55.84 cents a gallon, off 0.18 cent.
The complex closed the week with a yawn after rallying - for the second time this month - on the day of stocks data that most traders considered bearish, or neutral at best.
Thursday's rally followed Tuesday's 84-cent tumble, basis July, and topped off a week that was expected to have little feature in its business.
Traders said most of the action - either up or down - has been motivated more by chart points and external factors than supply and demand.
They pointed to the week's CFTC Commitment of Traders report and its evidence of an overwhelming speculative long presence in the market for Tuesday's drop.
They cited speculative money again on Thursday for the rally that ensued when a chart gap was filled.

"It's a really strange market," said Bob MacMinn, president of MPAS in Toronto. "Even in a market that's excessively long, according to the last CFTC report, we're not really stepping on this thing a lot from the short side."
MacMinn said fundamentals of the market are "pretty compellingly bearish", noting data that showed "high crude runs...product yields and their impact on stocks."

Unleaded gasoline, in the waning days of its peak demand period - from the futures market's perspective - has been no help to the complex. "Products have really just been along the ride," MacMinn said.
"In the past two months it's been a two-sided, choppy, technical market with an upside bias. It's stumped me," he said.
Traders will keep one eye on the United Nations next week.

With a week to go before the Iraqi-U.N oil-for-food accord expires, the first steps for renewing the deal will occur on Monday, when Secretary General Kofi Annan submit his recommendation on the pact's renewal to the Security Council.

The Council is expected to act on the report before the 180-day deal expires June 7. Although the accord is expected to be renewed, there is uncertainty over whether Washington will raise last-minute issues.
July crude will find support on the charts beginning at Thursday's low of $20.57, and graduating down to a gap between $20.40 and $20.50.
Resistance was pegged initially at $21.65, again at $22.15, the session highs of both May 19 and 20, and then at the $22.43 high posted in the May 16 rally.
Technical analysts see a retest of contract highs at $23.30 if momentum carries July through the latter resistance levels.
((--C. Thompson New York Energy Desk 212.859.1761))
